title: Trump lands in Manila with trade deals in sight and nuclear talks ahead
html:
A student marches against US President Donald Trump's participation in the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila.

PHOTO: REUTERS

AI generated

MANILA – US President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Nov 17, where he is scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the American aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.

Manila is Trump’s first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un.

The visit marks Trump’s first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Trump’s first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington’s oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home.

He will be feted later on Nov 17 at a gala as the “guest of honour” at the annual summit of the Association of South-east Asian Nations (ASEAN).

ASEAN’s leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have particularly escalated in recent years between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.

Ahead of Trump’s arrival, thousands of protesters faced off with riot shield-wielding police while carrying banners reading “Trump out now” and “Reject Pax Silica”, a reference to a US supply chain initiative that has divided opinions in the Philippines.

Meetings blitz

Trump’s streamlined agenda will send him straight to a meeting of the so-called Quad security alliance, with India’s Narendra Modi, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan and Australia’s Anthony Albanese.

While the Quad – broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence – has quietly progressed in deepening coordination, the short time allotted for the meeting on Nov 17 means it is unlikely to extend beyond pleasantries, Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution said.

The timing, however, carries significance, he said, given the historical meeting Trump will attend with the leaders of China and Russia in just two days.

“It’s a way of inoculating Trump against criticism of caving to authoritarians when he meets with Xi (Jinping) and (Vladimir) Putin in Shenzhen,” Hass said.

Hayley Channer, economic security director at the Sydney-based United States Studies Centre, said Trump’s decision to include ASEAN on his travel agenda is noteworthy.

“South-east Asia has never been a high priority for the United States, so President Trump travelling to Manila is significant,” she said.

A spokesman for Japan’s Foreign Ministry said the Quad agenda would include discussions of the East and South China Sea, areas where multiple parties have overlapping claims with China.

Trump will later attend a meeting with ASEAN heads of state before going to a gala dinner.

Tariffs and chips

While ASEAN leaders have spent three days grappling with a raft of regional issues, the spectre of Trump’s ongoing tariff blitz has loomed large.

Chinese Prime Minister Li Qiang slammed on Nov 16 what he called a “countercurrent of unilateralism and protectionism” while touting Beijing’s own expanding trade with the bloc.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Canada’s Mark Carney sang a similar tune on trade, with both explicitly citing a need to wean themselves off dependence on the American market.

Trump’s arrival on Nov 17 comes on the heels of an announced US rules shift on the transfer of advanced AI chips, a move that could potentially rankle ASEAN members.

Companies shipping high-end chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will now require a special licence, as the countries were said to represent a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion”.

Singapore responded by saying it is now exploring ways to facilitate “trusted access” for firms based in the city state.

Pax Silica

Trump is set to meet with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the presidential palace on Nov 18 before heading to Shenzhen.

Channer, from the US Studies Centre, said while presidents routinely focus on foreign affairs as their terms wind down, Trump’s sit-down is “more likely because the US is trying to further its Pax Silica initiative to build a complete mine-to-chip supply chain”.

Aimed at countering China’s dominance in semiconductors and rare earths, the initiative has been the focus of months of protests, as its flagship 1,620ha AI manufacturing hub north of Manila threatens to displace indigenous families.

“We are gathered here today to call for the stop of Pax Silica and to save the lands of the Filipino people,” Mariposa, a 21-year-old drag queen, said at a protest on Nov 17 while wearing a long black cape emblazoned with the words “Pax Silica Sashay Away!”.

US Ambassador Lee Lipton, a Trump appointee, earlier released a statement saying a long-rumoured deal signing for the site would not take place during the president’s visit. AFP, AP
summary: President Trump’s brief meeting with Quad leaders is unlikely to go beyond pleasantries, an analyst says.
